decision.reason: The supplied primary report (https://osf.io/download/n32zj/) has an unresolved internal target-identity and statistical contradiction: while its title header names Oberauer (2008, JEP:LMC, 'How to Say No: Single- and Dual-Process Theories of Short-Term Recognition Tested on Negative Probes'), its Introduction explicitly states that 'The present study will attempt to replicate the findings of Oberauer (2003) by testing the SP and DP model using the a modified Sternberg task', its References cite only Oberauer (2003, Journal of Memory and Language, 49, 469-483) and omit Oberauer (2008) entirely, and its Table 2 original list-length statistic (F(1, 31) = 18.7, p < .001, eta_p^2 = .38) conflicts with the RPP Master Dataset Table's Study 19 original statistic for Oberauer (2008) Experiment 3 (F(1, 31) = 14.2, p < .001, eta_p^2 = .31). In addition, the report's Discussion states both that the second analysis was 'partially replicated' and that the study 'failed to replicate the specific results found in the original study in regard to the accuracy measures' while remaining 'in line with the original paper's conclusion favouring the Dual-Process Model.' Because the primary report cannot be reliably attributed to the requested 2008 original study, the outcome is undeterminable.

decision.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Based on the a priori criterion, the replication was not successful. However, the effect was close to significance (p = .086) and the effect sizes was not significantly different from the original effect. At the same time, the other main finding of the paper (power ratings are correlated with profits) was significant (p = .01). To a certain extent, the original choice of the a priori criterion was arbitrary because neither correlation was held up by the original authors as “the” important correlation. Therefore, readers may want to avoid over-interpreting the dichotomous “replicated” versus “not replicated” criterion in this case. It should also be noted that the design of the original experiment did not allow us to increase the statistical power of the study. Commentary Overall, the findings of this replication were consistent with the original study, even though the a priori criterion was not met.
decision.location: Primary Project Report 76 (https://osf.io/download/4peq6/, Rule & Ambady, 2008), Confirmatory Analysis and Discussion (Summary of Replication Attempt & Commentary)
decision.reason: In the primary replication report for Rule and Ambady (2008), the authors test both main correlations from the original study alongside the two-factor trait structure. While the pre-selected focal correlation between leadership ratings and company profits fell just short of statistical significance (r(41) = .27, p = .086; 'Based on the a priori criterion, the replication was not successful', and exploratory removal of the Exxon outlier rendered both correlations non-significant), the other main correlation between power ratings and company profits was statistically significant (r(41) = .37, p = .01), the two-factor structure of trait ratings was replicated, and the Commentary notes that 'Overall, the findings of this replication were consistent with the original study, even though the a priori criterion was not met' while the Summary cautions against 'over-interpreting the dichotomous "replicated" versus "not replicated" criterion in this case.' Because the failure statement is explicitly qualified to an arbitrary single criterion while one main correlation failed to reach significance and the other main correlation succeeded, the overall outcome across tested original findings is mixed.

decision.quote:
A recent genome-wide association study by the International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium (IMSGC) reported
association of 17 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 14 loci with multiple sclerosis (MS). Only two loci, HLA-DRA
and IL2RA, reached genome-wide significance (Po5E08). In our study, we determined whether we could replicate the results
of the IMSGC and whether more SNPs are genome-wide significantly associated with MS. We assessed the association between
the 17 IMSGC SNPs and MS in three cohorts (total number of subjects 3981, among these 1853 cases). We performed a
meta-analysis of the results of our study, the original IMSGC results and the results of a recent replication study performed in
the Australian population. Of the 17 IMSGC SNPs, five SNPs showed genome-wide significant association with MS: HLA-DRA
(P¼8E124), IL7R (P¼6E09), IL2RA (P¼1E11), CD58 (P¼4E09) and CLEC16A (P¼3E12).Therefore, genome-wide
significance has now been shown for SNPs in different non-HLA MS risk genes.
decision.reason: Hoppenbrouwers et al. (2009) tested all 17 top candidate SNPs reported in the initial IMSGC (2007, 10.1056/nejmoa073493) genome-wide association study across three independent multiple sclerosis cohorts and a combined analysis of 11,376 individuals. While 5 SNPs reached genome-wide significance (HLA-DRA, IL7R, IL2RA, CD58, and CLEC16A) and EVI5 was independently replicated, the remaining tested IMSGC SNPs did not reach genome-wide significance, and for three IMSGC loci (PDE4B, DBC1, and ANKRD15) the authors explicitly report on p. 677 that 'our results suggest that the previously reported association in the initial IMSGC screen was a false positive association.' Because some tested original loci from IMSGC (2007) replicated and others failed as false positives, the paper-level outcome is mixed.

decision.location: Section 2.3 Discussion of Study 1 (p. 11), Section 3.3.1 Fraction-Test Results & Table 3 (pp. 20-22), and Section 3.4 Discussion of Study 2 (pp. 26-28)
decision.reason: Babari et al. (2025) replicate and extend Braithwaite and Siegler (2018, 10.1037/xlm0000546) across a textbook analysis (Study 1) and behavioral experiments with 6th graders (Study 2). In Study 1, the authors find nonrandom relations between operations and operand features in Swiss textbooks, but explicitly note that the fraction distributions are 'slightly different from the results presented by Braithwaite and Siegler (2018)' because Swiss addition/subtraction problems overwhelmingly use unequal rather than equal denominators. In Study 2 (Table 3 and Section 3.3.1), while most textbook-distribution predictions and the exploratory cluster pattern replicated, several specific predictions on the Fraction-Test were explicitly disconfirmed (marked 'X' in Table 3: Task 1 generating equal denominators more often for +/- than x/div; Task 5 choosing x/div over +/- for fraction-natural number pairs, where children unexpectedly favored +/-) or non-significant (marked '†' in Table 3 in Tasks 1, 2, and 4). Because tested original predictions show a combination of confirmed and disconfirmed/null findings across both studies, the overall outcome is mixed.
